Overview: Chickenpox is a human herpesvirus type 3 infection. Chickenpox is characterized by contagious rash that lasts up to 7 days. Chickenpox is highly contagious and spreads primarily through airborne droplets from inhalation and the mouth. Chickenpox continues to pose a public health challenge.
Symptoms: Pruritic red macules turning vesicular, crops of spots to blisters to crusts, intense itching, fever before rash.
Causes: Chickenpox is caused exclusively by primary infection with the Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV). It is a double-stranded DNA neurotropic alpha herpesvirus. Transmission primarily occurs through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles shed from an infected person. This systemic spread leads to the widespread, asynchronous rashes. Several factors can increase susceptibility or influence disease severity, though the direct cause remains VZV exposure. Neonates and immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk for severe and complicated infections. Exposure during pregnancy can lead to serious risks for both the mother and the fetus.
Preventions: Vaccination is the most effective method for preventing chickenpox
Treatment: Most healthy children with chickenpox require only symptomatic treatment, as the disease is typically self-limiting. The primary goals of treatment are to alleviate symptoms and prevent secondary bacterial infections
When to See a Doctor: Seek immediate medical attention if: **High-risk individuals:** The infected person is an infant (especially under 1 month), pregnant, immunocompromised, or an adult, as these groups are at higher risk for severe disease and complications
